### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","0"],["data-note-id","sib-i"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
<i lang="sr">
k, g, h
</i>
soften before
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
These three hard consonants don't sit comfortably next to a bright
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
. They shift to softer cousins —
<i lang="sr">
c, z, s
</i>
— that match the vowel better.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
juna
<span class="lit">
k
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
juna
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
jezi
<span class="lit">
k
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
jezi
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
mona
<span class="lit">
h
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
mona
<span class="lit">
si
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","1"],["data-note-id","gen-pl"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
Spacer
<i lang="sr">
-a
</i>
, and the old
<i lang="sr">
-iju
</i>
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
A stem that ends in two consonants slips an
<i lang="sr">
-a
</i>
between them before the ending: sister → of sisters, letter → of letters. A handful of nouns instead keep an old
<i lang="sr">
-iju
</i>
in place of
<i lang="sr">
-a
</i>
: eyes, ears, guests, fingers.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
sestra
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
sest
<span class="lit">
a
</span>
ra
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
pis
<span class="lit">
mo
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
pis
<span class="lit">
ama
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
viljuška
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
viljuš
<span class="lit">
a
</span>
ka
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
stak
<span class="lit">
lo
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
stak
<span class="lit">
ala
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
o
<span class="lit">
ko
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>

### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","2"],["data-note-id","sib-i"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
<i lang="sr">
k, g, h
</i>
soften before the
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
ending
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
When the feminine singular ending
<i lang="sr">

</i>
lands on a stem ending in
<i lang="sr">

</i>
,
<i lang="sr">
g
</i>
, or
<i lang="sr">
h
</i>
, those hard consonants shift to
<i lang="sr">
c, z, s
</i>
— softer sounds that sit better next to the
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">

</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">

<span class="lit">

</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">

<span class="lit">

</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
ru
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
Ameri
<span class="lit">
ka
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
Ameri
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>

### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","3"],["data-note-id","animacy"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
Living things vs everything else
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
In the masculine singular only, the accusative splits by whether the noun is alive. Living things (people, animals) take
<i lang="sr">
-a
</i>
— the same shape as the genitive. Inanimate things take
<i lang="sr">
-∅
</i>
— the nominative form, unchanged. So you reuse two endings you already know.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
pilot
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
pilot
<span class="lit">
a
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
grad
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
grad
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","4"],["data-note-id","palatal"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
<i lang="sr">
k, g, h
</i>
turn into
<i lang="sr">
č, ž, š
</i>
when calling out
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
When you address someone whose word ends in
<i lang="sr">
k
</i>
,
<i lang="sr">
g
</i>
, or
<i lang="sr">
h
</i>
, those consonants shift to their soft cousins —
<i lang="sr">
č, ž, š
</i>
— before the
<i lang="sr">
-e
</i>
ending. The hard sounds soften because you're calling, not stating.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
juna
<span class="lit">
k
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
juna
<span class="lit">
če
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
Bo
<span class="lit">
g
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
Bo
<span class="lit">
že
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
du
<span class="lit">
h
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
du
<span class="lit">
še
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","4"],["data-note-id","soft"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
After soft consonants, use
<i lang="sr">
-u
</i>
instead of
<i lang="sr">
-e
</i>
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
If the word already ends in a soft consonant —
<i lang="sr">
c, ć, č, đ, dž, j, lj, nj, š, ž
</i>
— adding a soft
<i lang="sr">
-e
</i>
on top would feel doubled. The ending switches to
<i lang="sr">
-u
</i>
instead.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
prijatelj
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
prijatelj
<span class="lit">
u
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
mladić
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
mladić
<span class="lit">
u
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
muž
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
muž
<span class="lit">
u
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","4"],["data-note-id","vok-f-name"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
Names usually keep their
<i lang="sr">
-a
</i>
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
Common nouns take
<i lang="sr">
-o
</i>
. Personal names normally stay unchanged when you call them, and diminutives in
<i lang="sr">
-ica
</i>
switch to
<i lang="sr">
-e
</i>
. Putting
<i lang="sr">
-o
</i>
on a name sounds formal or folkloric.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
žen
<span class="lit">
a
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
žen
<span class="lit">
o
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
Marija
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
Marija
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
sestric
<span class="lit">
a
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
sestric
<span class="lit">
e
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","5"],["data-note-id","soft-em"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
After soft consonants,
<i lang="sr">
-om
</i>
becomes
<i lang="sr">
-em
</i>
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
The round
<i lang="sr">
-om
</i>
feels heavy when it follows a soft consonant (
<i lang="sr">
c, ć, č, đ, dž, j, lj, nj, š, ž
</i>
). It thins to
<i lang="sr">
-em
</i>
so the word stays balanced — soft consonant, soft vowel.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
muž
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
muž
<span class="lit">
em
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
nož
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
nož
<span class="lit">
em
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
mesec
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
mesec
<span class="lit">
em
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
### popover [data-note-trigger]|[["data-case-idx","6"],["data-note-id","sib-i"],["data-note-trigger",null]]
<article class="note-pop">
<h4 class="note-title">
<i lang="sr">
k, g, h
</i>
soften before
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
(same as Dative)
</h4>
<p class="note-body">
The Locative singular ending for feminines is
<i lang="sr">
-i
</i>
— exactly the same as Dative. Same ending, same softening:
<i lang="sr">
k, g, h
</i>
become
<i lang="sr">
c, z, s
</i>
when they meet it.
</p>
<ul class="note-pairs">
<li>

<span class="lit">
ka
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">

</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
ru
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
knji
<span class="lit">
ga
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
knji
<span class="lit">
zi
</span>
</span>
</li>
<li>
<span class="from" lang="sr">
Ameri
<span class="lit">
ka
</span>
</span>
<span aria-hidden="true" class="arrow">
→
</span>
<span class="to" lang="sr">
Ameri
<span class="lit">
ci
</span>
</span>
</li>
</ul>
</article>
